name: Physics
topics: Module 8: From the universe to the atom
note: Written for the 2017 Physics syllabus, which HSC 2027 still uses. Check equations and constants against the HSC data sheet.

cards.f: Why are the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile treated separately?
cards.b: They are independent. Ignoring air resistance, horizontal velocity is constant (no horizontal force) and vertical motion has constant acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² downwards.

cards.f: Components of a launch velocity u at angle θ above the horizontal.
cards.b: Horizontal ux = u cos θ. Vertical uy = u sin θ.

cards.f: Time of flight for a projectile landing at its launch height.
cards.b: t = 2u sin θ / g.

cards.f: Maximum height of a projectile.
cards.b: At the top the vertical velocity is zero, so vy² = uy² + 2ay gives h = (u sin θ)² / 2g.

cards.f: Range of a projectile landing at its launch height.
cards.b: R = ux × t = u² sin 2θ / g. It is greatest at 45°.

cards.f: Which pairs of launch angles give the same range?
cards.b: Complementary angles, e.g. 30° and 60°, because sin 2θ is the same for both.

cards.f: Describe the velocity and acceleration at the top of a projectile's path.
cards.b: Velocity is horizontal (vertical component zero), not zero. Acceleration is still g downwards.

cards.f: Equations of motion used for projectiles.
cards.b: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as. Use them separately for the horizontal (a = 0) and vertical (a = −9.8) directions.

cards.f: How does air resistance change a projectile's path?
cards.b: Lower maximum height and shorter range, and the path is no longer a symmetrical parabola: it comes down more steeply.

cards.f: Define uniform circular motion.
cards.b: Motion in a circle at constant speed. The velocity keeps changing direction, so the object is accelerating towards the centre.

cards.f: Centripetal acceleration and force.
cards.b: a = v²/r and F = mv²/r, both directed towards the centre of the circle.

cards.f: Speed of an object in uniform circular motion in terms of period.
cards.b: v = 2πr / T.

cards.f: Angular velocity.
cards.b: ω = Δθ/Δt in rad/s, and v = rω.

cards.f: What provides the centripetal force for a car turning on a flat road?
cards.b: Friction between the tyres and the road. If more is needed than friction can give, the car skids outwards along a tangent.

cards.f: Why are curved roads banked?
cards.b: Part of the normal force then points towards the centre, so the car can turn with less need for friction. At the design speed, tan θ = v²/rg and no friction is needed.

cards.f: What happens to an object on a string if the string breaks during circular motion?
cards.b: It moves off in a straight line along the tangent, at the speed it had (Newton's first law).

cards.f: Torque.
cards.b: τ = r F sin θ: the turning effect of a force, where r is the distance from the pivot and θ the angle between r and F.

cards.f: Is work done by a centripetal force?
cards.b: No. The force is perpendicular to the motion, so W = Fs cos 90° = 0 and the speed (kinetic energy) does not change.

cards.f: Newton's law of universal gravitation.
cards.b: F = GMm / r², where G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² and r is the distance between the centres.

cards.f: Gravitational field strength at distance r from a planet's centre.
cards.b: g = GM / r².

cards.f: Orbital velocity of a satellite.
cards.b: Set gravity equal to the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = sqrt(GM/r). It does not depend on the satellite's mass.

cards.f: Kepler's third law.
cards.b: r³/T² = GM / 4π², the same for every body orbiting the same central mass.

cards.f: Gravitational potential energy (from infinity).
cards.b: U = −GMm / r. It is zero at infinity and negative everywhere else.

cards.f: Escape velocity.
cards.b: The launch speed needed to reach infinity: ½mv² = GMm/r, so v = sqrt(2GM/r).

cards.f: Total energy of a satellite in a circular orbit.
cards.b: E = KE + U = ½(GMm/r) − GMm/r = −GMm/2r.

cards.f: Low Earth orbit versus geostationary orbit.
cards.b: LEO: roughly 160 to 2000 km up, period about 90 minutes, used for imaging and the ISS. Geostationary: about 36 000 km up, 24-hour period above the equator, so it stays over one point (communications, weather).

cards.f: Why does a satellite's speed increase if it moves to a lower orbit?
cards.b: v = sqrt(GM/r): smaller r means greater speed, even though its total energy is lower.

cards.f: Electric field strength between two parallel plates.
cards.b: E = V/d, uniform between the plates, pointing from positive to negative.

cards.f: Force on a charge in an electric field.
cards.b: F = qE. A positive charge accelerates along the field; a negative charge against it.

cards.f: Work done on a charge moved through a potential difference.
cards.b: W = qV, which equals the gain in kinetic energy if no other forces act: ½mv² = qV.

cards.f: Path of a charged particle entering a uniform electric field at right angles.
cards.b: A parabola, like a projectile: constant velocity along the plates and constant acceleration across them.

cards.f: Force on a charge moving in a magnetic field.
cards.b: F = qvB sin θ. It is perpendicular to both v and B, so it changes direction but not speed.

cards.f: Path of a charged particle moving at right angles to a uniform magnetic field.
cards.b: A circle: qvB = mv²/r, so r = mv / qB.

cards.f: Why does a magnetic field do no work on a moving charge?
cards.b: The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so the speed and kinetic energy do not change.

cards.f: Force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field (the motor effect).
cards.b: F = lIB sin θ, where θ is the angle between the wire and the field. Direction by the right-hand palm rule.

cards.f: Force between two parallel current-carrying wires.
cards.b: F/l = μ0 I1 I2 / 2πr. Currents in the same direction attract; opposite directions repel.

cards.f: How is the ampere connected to the force between parallel wires?
cards.b: It was historically defined as the current that gives 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre between two wires 1 m apart (μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷).

cards.f: Define magnetic flux.
cards.b: Φ = BA cos θ (B A⊥), measured in webers, where θ is the angle between B and the normal to the area.

cards.f: Faraday's law.
cards.b: The induced emf equals the rate of change of flux linkage: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt.

cards.f: Lenz's law.
cards.b: The induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change in flux that caused it. It follows from conservation of energy.

cards.f: What are eddy currents and one use?
cards.b: Circulating currents induced in a conductor by a changing flux. They oppose the motion, used in magnetic braking (trains, roller coasters) and induction cooktops.

cards.f: Ideal transformer equation.
cards.b: Vp/Vs = Np/Ns = Is/Ip. A step-up transformer has more secondary turns.

cards.f: Why do real transformers lose energy, and how is it reduced?
cards.b: Eddy currents in the core (laminated core), resistance heating in the coils (thick copper), and flux leakage (coils wound together on a closed core).

cards.f: Why is electricity transmitted at very high voltage?
cards.b: For the same power, higher V means lower current, and power loss in the lines is P = I²R, so much less energy is wasted.

cards.f: Torque on a coil in a DC motor.
cards.b: τ = nIAB sin θ, where θ is the angle between the field and the normal to the coil. Maximum when the coil plane is parallel to the field.

cards.f: Role of the split-ring commutator in a DC motor.
cards.b: It reverses the current in the coil every half turn so the torque keeps turning the coil the same way.

cards.f: What is back emf in a motor?
cards.b: As the coil spins it cuts flux, inducing an emf opposing the supply. It grows with speed, so current is large at start-up and smaller at full speed.

cards.f: Why do motors burn out if jammed?
cards.b: No rotation means no back emf, so a large current flows through the coils and overheats them.

cards.f: How does an AC induction motor work?
cards.b: AC in the stator makes a rotating magnetic field. It induces currents in the squirrel-cage rotor, and the force on those currents drags the rotor round slightly slower than the field.

cards.f: DC generator versus AC generator.
cards.b: Both spin a coil in a field. A DC generator uses a split-ring commutator so the output does not reverse; an AC generator uses slip rings, so the output alternates.

cards.f: What did Maxwell's equations predict?
cards.b: Electromagnetic waves: oscillating electric and magnetic fields at right angles, travelling at c = 1/sqrt(μ0 ε0) ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s, so light is an EM wave.

cards.f: Wave equation for light.
cards.b: c = fλ.

cards.f: What does a continuous spectrum versus a line spectrum tell you?
cards.b: A hot dense object gives a continuous spectrum. A hot low-pressure gas gives bright emission lines; cool gas in front of a hot source gives dark absorption lines, both unique to each element.

cards.f: What can a star's spectrum tell us?
cards.b: Surface temperature, chemical composition, radial (Doppler) velocity, rotation, and density (line width).

cards.f: Wien's law.
cards.b: λmax = b / T, where b = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m K. Hotter objects peak at shorter wavelengths.

cards.f: How did Fizeau or Foucault measure the speed of light?
cards.b: With a rapidly turning toothed wheel (Fizeau) or rotating mirror (Foucault): the time for light to travel to a distant mirror and back was found from the rotation, giving about 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

cards.f: Young's double-slit experiment: what does it show?
cards.b: Bright and dark fringes from interference, which only waves do, so light is a wave. Fringe spacing Δy = λL/d.

cards.f: Condition for bright fringes in double-slit interference or a diffraction grating.
cards.b: d sin θ = mλ, where m = 0, 1, 2, … (path difference is a whole number of wavelengths).

cards.f: What is polarisation, and what does it show about light?
cards.b: Restricting the oscillation to one plane. Only transverse waves can be polarised, so light is transverse.

cards.f: Malus's law.
cards.b: I = Imax cos² θ, where θ is the angle between the light's polarisation and the polariser's axis.

cards.f: Newton's corpuscular model versus Huygens' wave model.
cards.b: Newton: light is particles, explaining straight-line travel and reflection; predicted light speeds up in water. Huygens: light is a wave; predicted it slows in water. Foucault showed light is slower in water.

cards.f: What was the ultraviolet catastrophe?
cards.b: Classical physics predicted a black body would give out infinite energy at short wavelengths. Planck solved it by quantising energy: E = hf.

cards.f: Planck's equation.
cards.b: E = hf, where h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Energy is emitted in packets (quanta).

cards.f: Describe the photoelectric effect.
cards.b: Light above a threshold frequency ejects electrons from a metal instantly. Below it, no electrons, however bright the light. Brighter light gives more electrons, not faster ones.

cards.f: Einstein's photoelectric equation.
cards.b: Kmax = hf − φ, where φ is the work function. The threshold frequency is f0 = φ/h.

cards.f: Why did the photoelectric effect support a particle model of light?
cards.b: Energy depends on frequency, not intensity, and there is no delay: each photon gives all its energy to one electron.

cards.f: What does the stopping voltage tell you in a photoelectric experiment?
cards.b: The maximum kinetic energy of the electrons: Kmax = qV(stop). A graph of Kmax against f has gradient h and x-intercept f0.

cards.f: Einstein's two postulates of special relativity.
cards.b: 1) The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames. 2) The speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers.

cards.f: Time dilation equation.
cards.b: t = t0 / sqrt(1 − v²/c²), where t0 is the proper time measured in the frame where the events happen at one place.

cards.f: Length contraction equation.
cards.b: l = l0 sqrt(1 − v²/c²), where l0 is the proper length measured at rest relative to the object. Contraction is only along the motion.

cards.f: Evidence for time dilation.
cards.b: Muons made in the upper atmosphere reach the ground because their lifetime is dilated, and atomic clocks flown on planes or GPS satellites run at different rates.

cards.f: Relativistic momentum.
cards.b: p = m0 v / sqrt(1 − v²/c²). It grows without limit as v approaches c, so nothing with mass reaches c.

cards.f: Mass-energy equivalence.
cards.b: E = mc². Mass is a form of energy; a small mass defect releases a large amount of energy.

cards.f: What was the significance of the Michelson-Morley experiment?
cards.b: It found no change in light speed with Earth's motion, so no evidence of an aether. This supported Einstein's second postulate.

cards.f: Evidence for the Big Bang.
cards.b: Galaxies receding (Hubble's law, redshift), the cosmic microwave background radiation, and the observed amounts of hydrogen and helium.

cards.f: Hubble's law.
cards.b: v = H0 d: a galaxy's recession speed is proportional to its distance, showing the universe is expanding.

cards.f: What happened in the first few minutes after the Big Bang?
cards.b: As the universe cooled, quarks formed protons and neutrons, then nuclei of hydrogen and helium formed. Atoms only formed about 380 000 years later when electrons could join nuclei.

cards.f: Describe the main sequence on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram.
cards.b: A band from hot, bright, blue stars (top left) to cool, dim, red stars (bottom right) where stars fuse hydrogen to helium in their cores.

cards.f: Proton-proton chain versus CNO cycle.
cards.b: Both fuse hydrogen into helium. The p-p chain dominates in stars like the Sun; the CNO cycle, with carbon as a catalyst, dominates in hotter, more massive stars.

cards.f: Where do elements heavier than iron come from?
cards.b: Neutron capture in supernovae and neutron star mergers. Fusion beyond iron absorbs energy rather than releasing it.

cards.f: What did Thomson's cathode ray experiment show?
cards.b: Cathode rays are negative particles (electrons). Balancing electric and magnetic deflection gave their charge-to-mass ratio: q/m = E / (B² r).

cards.f: What did Millikan's oil drop experiment show?
cards.b: Charge is quantised: every drop's charge was a whole-number multiple of e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

cards.f: Rutherford's gold foil experiment: result and conclusion.
cards.b: Most alpha particles went straight through, a few bounced back. So the atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.

cards.f: What was Chadwick's contribution?
cards.b: He discovered the neutron (1932): neutral radiation from beryllium knocked protons out of paraffin, and only a neutral particle with about a proton's mass fitted conservation of momentum and energy.

cards.f: Bohr's model of the atom.
cards.b: Electrons orbit in fixed energy levels without radiating. They emit or absorb a photon of energy E = hf only when jumping between levels.

cards.f: Rydberg equation for hydrogen.
cards.b: 1/λ = R(1/nf² − 1/ni²), where R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹. Transitions to n = 2 give the visible Balmer series.

cards.f: Limitations of Bohr's model.
cards.b: It only worked for hydrogen-like atoms, could not explain the different brightness of lines or the splitting in magnetic fields, and mixed classical and quantum ideas without justification.

cards.f: de Broglie wavelength.
cards.b: λ = h / mv. Particles have wave properties. Electron orbits fit whole numbers of wavelengths.

cards.f: Evidence for matter waves.
cards.b: Davisson and Germer diffracted electrons off a nickel crystal and got an interference pattern matching the de Broglie wavelength.

cards.f: What did Schrödinger add?
cards.b: A wave equation for the electron. Electrons are described by probability clouds (orbitals) rather than fixed orbits.

cards.f: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
cards.b: Alpha: helium nucleus, very ionising, stopped by paper. Beta minus: electron from a neutron changing to a proton, stopped by aluminium. Gamma: high-energy photon, reduced by thick lead.

cards.f: Half-life equation.
cards.b: N = N0 e^(−λt), where λ = ln 2 / t½.

cards.f: Define mass defect and binding energy.
cards.b: Mass defect: the nucleus has less mass than its separate nucleons. Binding energy = Δm c², the energy needed to pull the nucleus apart.

cards.f: Why do both fission and fusion release energy?
cards.b: The products have a higher binding energy per nucleon (iron-56 is the peak), so mass is lost and released as energy.

cards.f: What is a chain reaction?
cards.b: In fission, each split nucleus releases neutrons that split more nuclei. Control rods absorb neutrons to keep it steady in a reactor.

cards.f: The Standard Model: what are the fundamental particles?
cards.b: Six quarks and six leptons (including the electron and neutrinos), force-carrying bosons (photon, gluon, W and Z), and the Higgs boson.

cards.f: Quark makeup of a proton and a neutron.
cards.b: Proton: up, up, down (charge +2/3 + 2/3 − 1/3 = +1). Neutron: up, down, down (charge 0).

cards.f: Why are particle accelerators needed to study the Standard Model?
cards.b: High-energy collisions turn kinetic energy into mass (E = mc²), creating heavy particles such as the Higgs boson, and probe very small distances.
